title: Redwood Security & Compliance Review - Acme Health
summary: Security and compliance deep-dive focused on SOC 2 / ISO posture, RBAC/SSO, audit logs and retention, encryption/KMS integration, data residency options, and explicit confirmation that customer prompts/content are not used to train models. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs for PHI/PII workloads and next steps to share SOC2 report, security whitepaper, and BAA conversation.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood here, with Maya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Lena Torres: Doing well, thanks. We've got a mix from security, legal, and platform on the line.
[00:10] Maya Patel: Hi, hi. Quick agenda: SOC 2 / ISO posture, RBAC/SSO, audit logs, encryption/KMS, data residency, and then data handling questions you sent — retention, PII/PHI, and whether we use customer data for training.
[00:20] Dr. Amir Shah: Perfect. We're particularly sensitive to PHI because a couple of POC use-cases will touch clinical notes. We need clarity on logs, retention, and BAAs.
[00:30] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We'll be transparent. I'll start with high level then Maya can dig into technical specifics.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II — we completed our last audit in Q4 2024, and we have ISO 27001 in progress, expect certificate mid-2025. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.
[01:35] Nicole Park: When you say "share under NDA" — we mean as part of our security review process, correct? We typically require the SOC 2 for vendors handling PHI.
[01:45] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's standard. We'll send the redacted SOC 2 Type II report and our compliance pack. We'll also include our security whitepaper and encryption architecture doc.
[02:12] Maya Patel: On RBAC and SSO — Redwood supports SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM for provisioning. You can map roles upstream; we have fine-grained RBAC in the Console and API keys can be scoped per team or route. For private and dedicated deployments we integrate with your IdP over the VPC control plane.
[03:00] Dr. Amir Shah: For SCIM, does that sync groups back, or is it one-way? We need group sync so engineers can be added by our directory.
[03:12] Maya Patel: SCIM is one-way (IdP to Redwood) for provisioning groups and users. We can map group attributes to RBAC roles. There are occasional edge-case mismatches, but we add custom attribute mapping.
[04:00] Samir Rao: Audit logs — what's the retention and the level of detail?
[04:07] Jordan Lee: Audit logs capture API calls, user management events, authentication events, and admin actions. By default hosted customers get 90 days of retention; enterprise tiers and dedicated/private customers can configure longer retention or ship logs to your SIEM (S3, Splunk, or via syslog).
[04:30] Dr. Amir Shah: We usually need immutable, append-only logs for 1 year for clinical audits. Can you do that?
[04:38] Maya Patel: Yes — dedicated and private options support long-term immutable retention. For hosted we can set up log export to your AWS account (S3 with object lock or Glacier) to meet the 1-year requirement. We can also provide signed timestamps for critical events.
[05:10] Nicole Park: Encryption — at rest and in transit? KMS? HSM?
[05:16] Maya Patel: TLS 1.2+ in transit. At rest we encrypt using AES-256. For encryption keys we integrate with customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) for dedicated and private; for hosted we offer our managed KMS by default but can configure CMKs if required. HSM-backed keys available for Private deployments.
[06:00] Lena Torres: Is key rotation supported and audited?
[06:06] Maya Patel: Yes. Key rotation for CMKs is supported and key usage events are logged in audit trails. We surface key rotation dates and can produce logs showing when each key was used for encryption/decryption.
[06:30] Jordan Lee: Now the data handling: prompt and content retention, PII/PHI, and whether we train on customer data. I know this is the big one.
[06:45] Dr. Amir Shah: Yes. Straight question: does Redwood use customer prompts or outputs to train our models or to improve base models?
[06:52] Jordan Lee: Short answer: no, we do not use customer prompts, responses, or content to train our public models.
[07:00] Maya Patel: To expand — by default hosted telemetry used for platform stability (errors, performance metrics) is collected. Customer content and prompts are not used to improve or retrain LMs. For customers that opt-in to data sharing for product improvement, that's an explicit opt-in and contract.
[07:20] Lena Torres: How is that enforced? Written? Technical enforcement? We need contractual commitments and technical controls.
[07:30] Jordan Lee: We'll include contractual language in our DPA that prohibits training on customer data unless explicitly consented. Technically, our pipelines keep a separation: model training buckets are separate, and ingestion pipelines for hosted customer content are blocked from model training workflows. For enterprise private deployments, you control the data plane entirely.
[08:00] Dr. Amir Shah: Okay. Is there an option to completely disable retention for prompts on hosted so nothing persists beyond the request handling?
[08:08] Maya Patel: For hosted, default short-term retention is 30 days for troubleshooting; we can offer a no-retention policy under enterprise terms where logs and content are not persisted beyond ephemeral processing. Alternatively, Dedicated or Private deployments offer zero-retention configurations by default because customer data stays in your VPC/on-prem.
[09:00] Samir Rao: For PHI, we need a BAA. Can Redwood sign BAAs?
[09:10] Jordan Lee: We can engage legal on that. For Private/Dedicated customers we routinely sign BAAs; for hosted customers we evaluate case-by-case—often offering dedicated clusters and extra controls. We'll flag legal to follow up.
[09:30] Nicole Park: We'll need specifics: data flows, who has access, subprocessors list.
[09:35] Jordan Lee: We'll attach our subprocessor list and data flow diagrams in the follow-up package.
[10:12] Maya Patel: On PII detection — we provide built-in optional redaction hooks and a PII detection engine that can run pre-request to redact or hash sensitive fields. You can run client-side redaction before sending, or we can apply server-side redaction rules.
[10:45] Dr. Amir Shah: Does the PII detector run inline? Any latency impact?
[10:50] Maya Patel: Minimal. It's designed to be lightweight; in our benchmarks inline redaction added ~10-30ms per request depending on payload size. For high-throughput flows you can batch or do client-side processing.
[11:20] Lena Torres: Auditability: can you show per-request metadata like requestor, timestamp, route, model variant, and whether the request hit a cache?
[11:30] Maya Patel: Yes — audit logs include requestor (API key or user), timestamp, route, model id/version, latency, token usage, and cache hit/miss. For sensitive workloads we can redact content in logs but still keep metadata.
[12:00] Jordan Lee: Another ask we get is 'how do you prove data wasn't used for training' — we provide signed attestation statements and can include pipeline diagrams and segregation controls.
[12:18] Nicole Park: Would you be willing to provide an attestation as part of contract?
[12:22] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can add a no-training attestation clause. Legal will propose language.
[13:05] Dr. Amir Shah: What about model snapshots or embeddings that might persist — are embeddings stored?
[13:12] Maya Patel: Embeddings are persisted only if you request persistent embedding storage (for search/recall). By default ephemeral embeddings are not persisted. If you use our embedding index service, that's a storage that you can control retention for or export.
[13:45] Samir Rao: We use customer-managed S3 for exported indexes?
[13:50] Maya Patel: We support exporting to your S3 or providing encryption-at-rest keys for storage. For private deployments everything can be kept on-prem.
[14:20] Jordan Lee: A couple of operational notes: we have per-route quotas, private networks, and a hardened runtime. For Dedicated clusters we can isolate compute tenancy, and for private deployments you own the control plane.
[15:00] Lena Torres: Incident response: what's your breach notification timeline and process?
[15:07] Jordan Lee: Standard: notify within 72 hours of detection for critical incidents, we'll provide root-cause analysis, remediation steps, and coordinate with your security team. We also have playbooks and SOC contacts.
[16:00] Nicole Park: SLA impact for incidents — do you provide credits?
[16:05] Jordan Lee: For enterprise contracts we include SLA credits; details are contract-specific.
[16:30] Dr. Amir Shah: Pen testing — do you accept customer-initiated tests?
[16:36] Maya Patel: Yes, after coordination. For hosted we require advance notice and a allowed test window; for private/dedicated you get more flexibility.
[17:00] Lena Torres: Where can we review docs now?
[17:05] Jordan Lee: We'll send the SOC2 Type II PDF, security whitepaper, encryption architecture, subprocessor list, DPA draft, and a short decision matrix comparing hosted/dedicated/private for PHI use. Links: https://redwood.ai/security (security whitepaper), https://redwood.ai/compliance (compliance pack).
[17:50] Nicole Park: Please label anything that's NDA-only.
[17:55] Jordan Lee: Will do.
[18:20] Samir Rao: Two quick technical questions — is KV cache persisted across restarts? And how is model fallback logged?
[18:28] Maya Patel: KV cache in the runtime is ephemeral in hosted; in dedicated/private we can persist warm snapshots to speed cold starts. Model fallback events are logged as part of the request trace with reason codes (capacity, latency, etc.).
[20:00] Dr. Amir Shah: For compliance reviews we also look for evidence of segregation of duties and least privilege. How do you demonstrate that?
[20:10] Maya Patel: We can provide screenshots plus role matrices from the console, and audit trails showing admin changes. Our internal ops has RBAC matrices segregating dev/test/prod.
[21:30] Lena Torres: Final set — data residency. We need EU-only processing for a subset of workloads. Is that possible?
[21:40] Jordan Lee: Yes. We have region affinity controls and can route requests to EU-only clusters. For strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private in-region deployments; hosted can be regional but may route through centralized control plane.
[22:15] Nicole Park: Can you provide a diagram of data flow for EU workloads showing control plane and data plane separation?
[22:20] Jordan Lee: Yes — that will be in the follow-up package.
[23:00] Maya Patel: One more note on logs: we can provide signed audit exports (time-stamped) for a given period if you need attested evidence for audits.
[24:00] Lena Torres: Great. Let's talk next steps and responsibilities.
[24:10] Jordan Lee: Sure — I'll summarize.
[24:22] Jordan Lee: Action items: we'll send SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA draft, security whitepaper, and a proposed BAA route. We'll also include technical docs on KMS integration and the no-training attestation.
[24:45] Nicole Park: Legal will review DPA/BAA, security will validate logs and redaction, platform will run a quick pilot.
[25:00] Jordan Lee: Timeline — can we aim to have the docs to you by next week and then schedule a follow-up in two weeks for any clarifications?
[25:10] Lena Torres: That works. We need to review the BAA quickly though.
[25:20] Jordan Lee: Understood.
[26:00] Maya Patel: Quick note — for immediate POC we can spin up a dedicated trial instance with logging disabled and export-only to your S3 so you can test PHI flows without persistence.
[26:25] Dr. Amir Shah: That would be ideal.
[27:10] Jordan Lee: Okay folks, thanks. We'll follow up with the package. Any other questions?
[27:20] Samir Rao: None from me.
[27:25] Nicole Park: All good.
[27:30] Lena Torres: Thanks everyone.
[27:35] Jordan Lee: Thanks, bye.
[27:40] [call ended (approx)]
